extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties involved in PTAB inter partes review (IPR) obviousness disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules applied in PTAB/ Federal Circuit obviousness analyses in IPRs, including how to evaluate objective indicia (secondary considerations), nexus, motivation to combine, and reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of nexus and burden shift
rubrics_metrics.description: “then a nexus is presumed and the burden shifts to the party asserting obviousness to present evidence to rebut the presumed nexus.”  Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. v. Philip Morris Inc., 229 F.3d 1120, 1130 (Fed. Cir. 2000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence of objective indicia is shown to be coextensive/commensurate in scope with the claimed invention, a presumption of nexus arises and the challenger must rebut it with evidence showing lack of nexus or that the indicia are attributable to something else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coextensiveness / commensurate-in-scope requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Coextensive “mean[s] that the product is the invention disclosed and claimed. . . . A product is essentially the claimed invention when, for example, the unclaimed features amount to nothing more than additional insignificant features.”  Campbell Soup Co. v. Gamon Plus, Inc., 10 F.4th 1268, 1276–77 (Fed. Cir. 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective-indicia evidence (e.g., a commercial product or clinical candidate) must be essentially the claimed invention — unclaimed differences must be insignificant — or else the evidence is not commensurate in scope and cannot support a presumption of nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia categories to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner relies on objective evidence of “(1) long-felt need for an effective gene therapy for hemophilia B and failure of others; (2) industry praise and copying; and (3) unexpectedly superior efficacy”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating secondary considerations, identify which indicia are asserted (e.g., long‑felt need, praise/copying, unexpected results) and assess whether each is supported and tied to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement tying objective indicia to what is claimed and novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Where objective indicia “result[ ] from something other than what is both claimed and novel in the claim, there is no nexus to the merits of the claimed invention.” (citing Merck & Cie v. Gnosis S.P.A., 808 F.3d 829, 837 (Fed. Cir. 2015)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective evidence directed to a feature that was already in the prior art (not the claimed novelty) cannot establish a nexus supporting non‑obviousness. The evidence must be tied to the novel features of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fox Factory alternative (direct proof of nexus via unique characteristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fox Factory provides, “[a] finding that a presumption of nexus is inappropriate does not end the inquiry into secondary considerations”; rather, “the patent owner is still afforded an opportunity to prove nexus by showing that the evidence of secondary considerations is the ‘direct result of the unique characteristics of the claimed invention.’”  Fox Factory, 994 F.3d at 1374 (quoting In re Huang, 100 F.3d 135, 140 (Fed. Cir. 1996)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without a presumption, patent owner may try to prove nexus directly by showing the asserted objective indicia are the direct result of unique characteristics of the claimed invention; must present argument and evidence of those unique characteristics and causal link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing objective indicia in context of the claimed invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ultimately, the fact finder must weigh the [objective indicia] evidence presented in the context of whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a skilled artisan.”  (citing Lectrosonics, Inc. v. Zaxcom, Inc., IPR2018-01129, Paper 33 at 33 (PTAB Jan. 24, 2020) (precedential)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations are not assessed in isolation; they are considered together with the Graham factors and the claimed invention as a whole to determine obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry praise and copying must be commensurate and specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner notes Patent Owner does not identify any specific evidence of copying beyond the adoption of the “Padua” designation; court agrees praise in the relied references was primarily directed to FIX‑R338L (a prior‑art component) and not commensurate with the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of praise or copying should specifically tie adoption/praise to the claimed invention as a whole; mere terminology adoption or praise for a component known in the prior art is insufficient to establish nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑felt need / failure of others must relate to claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner asserts Factor IX Padua was a “game‑changer” and industry adoption (including ongoing clinical trials) is evidence of satisfying the long‑felt need; Board found such evidence may be directed at the variant rather than the claimed combination and thus not commensurate with claim 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that a need existed and was unmet can support non‑obviousness only if the evidence is linked to the claimed invention (not merely to an element that was already known).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results — need for proper comparative baseline and comparable studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner asserts a 9‑fold increased activity of FIX‑R338L compared to wild‑type FIX was surprising relative to prior art showing 2–6 fold increases; Board found comparisons unpersuasive because results came from different types of studies (recombinant vs gene therapy) and lacked head‑to‑head comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To support unexpected results, show a convincing, head‑to‑head comparison to the closest prior art using comparable methods/data; differences in study types (in vitro vs in vivo) can undermine claimed unexpectedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of the evidence standard for petitioner in IPR obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: We find that Petitioner has shown by a preponderance of the evidence that the combinations ... teach the limitations of claim 1 ... and that a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine the references ... with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The challenger must prove obviousness by a preponderance of the evidence: show that prior art teaches claim limitations and that motivation and reasonable expectation to combine existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine must be supported by rational underpinnings (no hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner contends Petitioner's combination of references is based on hindsight. The Board: “We disagree ... Petitioner has shown a motivation to combine supported by rational underpinnings in the evidentiary record.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A demonstrated rationale (e.g., to improve efficacy by using a more active variant) and supporting testimony/documents are required to show a POSA would have been motivated to combine references; mere ex post reasoning is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success in unpredictable fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner contends a person of ordinary skill would not have had a reasonable expectation of success ... in view of the highly unpredictable field of gene therapy, Manno’s failure, and no AAV‑FIX‑R338L‑specific data (citing OSI Pharms., LLC v. Apotex Inc., 939 F.3d 1375, 1384–85 (Fed. Cir. 2019)). The Board disagreed, finding prior art teachings and expert testimony supported a reasonable expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the field is unpredictable, challenger must still show that the prior art and common knowledge provided a reasonable expectation of success; evidence such as analogous experiments, known properties, or expert testimony can supply that expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction influences disclosure and obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the adopted construction, “treating” a coagulopathy includes partial alleviation of symptoms, for any duration of therapeutic efficacy; thus Manno’s report of ten weeks without bleeding counted as “treating.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How terms are construed can determine whether prior art satisfies claim limitations — adopt and apply constructions explicitly in the obviousness inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of clinical adoption must be commensurate with claim scope (example: capsid/promoter breadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner argued AMT‑061 cannot provide evidence of objective indicia because it is not coextensive with the challenged claims (AMT‑061 uses a specific AAV5 capsid while the claims cover use of any AAV capsid), and claims permit many changes (promoters, capsids, FIX variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are broad (e.g., any capsid, many promoters, wide sequence identity ranges), evidence limited to a single implementation (one capsid, one promoter) may not be commensurate in scope and thus insufficient to establish nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations cannot be used to circumvent prior art showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner argues that Patent Owner cannot circumvent non‑obviousness evidence by circularly arguing no objective indicia are possible because the claimed invention was in the prior art. The Board states that because FIX‑R338L was available in the prior art, it cannot be the basis for finding a nexus with the claimed invention; see ClassCo, 838 F.3d at 1220.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the component credited for objective indicia was already publicly available in the prior art, the patent owner cannot attribute secondary considerations to that component to avoid obviousness findings — the indicia must relate to the claim’s novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of evidence and weight of a weak nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: In summary, Patent Owner does not meet its burden to show a presumption of nexus or show a nexus ... Weighing the evidence and arguments presented, we determine that even if there is some nexus, it is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when some connection exists between evidence and the claimed invention, the Board weighs the strength of the nexus; a weak or attenuated nexus will not overcome a showing of obviousness.
